name: Sweet potato
intro: A naturally sweet, soft first vegetable. It’s one of the foods the CDC lists as high in vitamin C, which helps your baby absorb iron.

serving.text: Steam, bake or roast until very soft, then puree or mash. Or offer thick wedges, peeled and soft enough to squash easily between your thumb and finger.
Mash with a fork, or offer soft, bite-sized cubes.
Serve soft cubes or wedges from the family meal, without added salt.

choking: Low risk when it’s cooked very soft. Avoid hard, undercooked pieces.

name: Carrot
intro: A sweet, mild vegetable that purees smoothly once it’s cooked soft.

serving.text: Steam or boil until very soft, then puree or mash. Or offer whole cooked sticks soft enough to squash easily between your thumb and finger.
Mash, or offer small, soft-cooked pieces.
Serve soft-cooked pieces or thin shreds. Keep raw carrot sticks away until your child chews well.

choking: Raw carrot is a choking hazard (CDC). Always cook carrot until soft, and never serve hard raw pieces or coins.

name: Broccoli
intro: A green vegetable the CDC lists as high in vitamin C, which helps your baby absorb iron from other foods.

serving.text: Steam until very soft and puree, or offer large florets with a stalk “handle” that are soft enough to squash easily between your thumb and finger.
Offer small, soft florets or chop finely and mix into other foods.
Serve soft, bite-sized florets from the family meal.

choking: Steam until soft. Raw or firm broccoli is hard to chew.

name: Peas
intro: Small, sweet and easy to keep in the freezer.

serving.text: Cook until soft and puree, or mash well.
Flatten each pea with a fork, or mash, so they aren’t whole and round.
Flatten or lightly mash peas until your child is chewing well.

choking: Whole, round peas can block a small airway. Mash or flatten them.

name: Spinach
intro: A dark leafy green. The CDC lists dark green leafy vegetables as a plant source of iron.

serving.text: Steam or wilt, then puree well and mix into other purees.
Chop cooked spinach finely and stir it into eggs, pasta or mashes.
Serve finely chopped in family meals.

choking: Low risk when cooked and finely chopped or pureed. Large raw leaves can be hard to manage.

name: Zucchini
intro: A mild, watery vegetable that cooks quickly.

serving.text: Steam until soft and puree, or offer thick spears soft enough to squash easily between your thumb and finger.
Offer soft-cooked half-moons or small pieces.
Serve soft-cooked pieces from family meals.

choking: Low risk when cooked soft.

name: Butternut squash
intro: A sweet, velvety squash that purees beautifully.

serving.text: Steam or roast until very soft, then puree or mash. Or offer soft wedges.
Mash, or offer soft, bite-sized cubes.
Serve soft cubes from family meals.

choking: Low risk when cooked very soft.

name: Green beans
intro: Long, easy-to-hold beans that turn soft when cooked.

serving.text: Steam until very soft and puree, or offer whole cooked beans soft enough to squash easily between your thumb and finger.
Cut soft-cooked beans into small pieces.
Serve soft-cooked, cut into small pieces.

choking: Cook until soft; firm or raw green beans are hard to chew.

name: Cauliflower
intro: A mild vegetable that mashes into a smooth, creamy texture.

serving.text: Steam until very soft and puree, or offer large soft florets.
Mash, or offer small, soft florets.
Serve soft, bite-sized florets.

choking: Steam until soft. Raw florets are hard to chew.

name: Kale
intro: A sturdy dark leafy green. The CDC lists dark green leafy vegetables as a plant source of iron.

serving.text: Remove the tough stems, steam until very soft, then puree well and mix into other purees.
Chop cooked kale finely and stir it into eggs, pasta or mashes.
Serve cooked and finely chopped in family meals.

choking: Raw kale is tough and hard to chew. Cook it soft and chop it finely or puree it.

name: Parsnips
intro: A naturally sweet root vegetable, a lot like carrot, that turns creamy once cooked.

serving.text: Peel, then steam, boil or roast until very soft and puree or mash. Or offer cooked sticks soft enough to squash easily between your thumb and finger.
Mash, or offer small, soft-cooked pieces.
Serve soft-cooked pieces from the family meal, without added salt.

choking: Raw parsnip is hard, like raw carrot. Always cook it until soft, and never serve hard raw pieces.

name: Haricots verts
intro: Thin, tender French green beans that cook quickly.

serving.text: Steam until very soft and puree, or offer whole cooked beans soft enough to squash easily between your thumb and finger.
Cut soft-cooked beans into small pieces.
Serve soft-cooked, cut into small pieces.

choking: Cook until soft; firm or raw beans are hard to chew.

name: Avocado
intro: Creamy, no-cook and full of healthy fats.

serving.text: Mash or puree until smooth, or offer thick spears of ripe avocado.
Offer mashed avocado or small, soft cubes.
Serve cubes, slices or spread on toast.

choking: Low risk when ripe and soft.

name: Banana
intro: Sweet, soft and needs no cooking.

serving.text: Mash until smooth, or offer half a banana with some peel left on as a handle.
Offer small, soft pieces or slices.
Serve slices or pieces.

choking: Low risk when ripe. Cut into pieces rather than offering large chunks once your baby bites off pieces.

name: Apple
intro: A sweet fruit that’s easy to steam and puree.

serving.text: Peel, steam or bake until very soft, then puree. Or offer soft-cooked wedges.
Offer soft-cooked pieces or grated raw apple.
Offer thin slices or grated apple. Wait until your child chews well before offering raw pieces.

choking: Raw, hard apple pieces are a choking hazard (CDC). Cook apple soft, or grate it, for babies and young toddlers.

name: Pear
intro: Soft, juicy and naturally sweet.

serving.text: Puree or mash ripe pear; steam it first if it’s firm.
Offer small pieces of very ripe or soft-cooked pear.
Serve soft slices or pieces.

choking: Firm, unripe pear is hard to chew. Use very ripe pear or cook it soft.

name: Blueberries
intro: Small, sweet berries. The CDC lists berries as high in vitamin C.

serving.text: Mash or puree, or stir smashed berries into yogurt or oatmeal.
Flatten each berry between your fingers, or quarter them.
Quarter or flatten berries until your child chews well.

choking: Whole blueberries are a choking hazard (CDC). Always mash, flatten or cut them.

name: Strawberries
intro: A sweet berry that’s high in vitamin C.

serving.text: Mash or puree ripe strawberries, or offer a very large, ripe berry to hold.
Cut into small pieces or thin slices.
Cut into small pieces.

choking: Small whole berries can block an airway. Mash or cut them into small pieces.

name: Mango
intro: Sweet, juicy and soft when ripe.

serving.text: Mash or puree ripe mango, or offer a large peeled strip.
Offer small, soft pieces.
Serve small pieces or slices.

choking: Low risk when ripe and soft. Avoid giving the slippery pit to suck on.

name: Peach
intro: A soft, sweet stone fruit.

serving.text: Peel and mash or puree ripe peach, or offer a large, ripe peeled slice.
Offer small, soft pieces.
Serve small pieces or slices.

choking: Remove the pit, and cut canned peaches into small pieces (CDC).

name: Cherries
intro: Sweet, juicy summer fruit. Remove the pits first, as they're a choking hazard.

serving.text: Remove the stems and pits, then puree or mash.
Remove the pits and cut cherries into quarters or small pieces.
Pit and quarter cherries until your child chews well.

choking: Whole cherries and cherry pits are choking hazards. Always remove the pits and stems, and mash or cut the fruit.

name: Prunes
intro: Dried plums with a deep, sweet flavor. Stewed and pureed, they mix well into oatmeal and yogurt.

serving.text: Simmer pitted prunes in water until very soft, then puree until smooth.
Stir prune puree into oatmeal, yogurt or other fruit purees.
Offer stewed prunes chopped into small pieces, or keep using the puree.

choking: Dried fruit is sticky and can be a choking hazard. Serve prunes stewed and pureed or finely chopped, never whole or dried.

name: Egg
intro: An easy, inexpensive protein. The CDC lists eggs among foods with iron.

serving.text: Hard-boil and mash the egg, or serve thin strips of a fully cooked omelet.
Offer small pieces of hard-boiled egg or scrambled egg.
Serve fully cooked eggs in small pieces.

choking: Low risk when soft and in small pieces. Always cook until both the yolk and white are firm.
allergenNote: Egg is one of the most common food allergens. Introduce it early, around 6 months, once your baby has had a few other first foods. Start with a small amount, offer only one new allergen at a time, and watch for a reaction. Once your baby tolerates it, keep offering it regularly. If your baby has severe eczema or another food allergy, talk to your pediatrician first. Call 911 right away for swelling of the lips or face, trouble breathing, or repeated vomiting.

name: Chicken
intro: A mild protein. The CDC lists poultry as a source of easily absorbed iron.

serving.text: Puree cooked chicken with a little water, breast milk or formula until smooth, or offer large, shredded strips.
Offer finely shredded or minced chicken.
Serve small, tender pieces.

choking: Tough or large chunks of meat are a choking hazard (CDC). Shred finely or puree, and cook to 165°F.

name: Beef
intro: Red meat is one of the richest sources of easily absorbed iron (CDC).

serving.text: Puree cooked beef until smooth, or offer soft, slow-cooked strips to suck on.
Offer finely minced or ground beef, or soft meatballs cut small.
Serve small, tender pieces or ground beef.

choking: Tough or large chunks of meat are a choking hazard (CDC). Cook ground beef to 160°F.

name: Turkey
intro: A mild poultry that’s a good source of iron (CDC).

serving.text: Puree cooked turkey until smooth, or offer large, soft shredded pieces.
Offer finely shredded or ground turkey.
Serve small, tender pieces.

choking: Shred finely and cook to 165°F. Avoid deli meat sticks and hot dogs (CDC).

name: Salmon
intro: A fatty fish the FDA lists as a “Best Choice” for children because it’s low in mercury.

serving.text: Flake cooked salmon and mash it with a little puree, checking carefully for bones.
Offer soft flakes your baby can pick up.
Serve flaked salmon or soft fish cakes.

choking: Remove every bone (CDC). Cook to 145°F, until it flakes easily.
allergenNote: Fish is a common food allergen. Introduce it early, around 6 months, once your baby has had a few other first foods. Start with a small amount, offer only one new allergen at a time, and watch for a reaction. Once your baby tolerates it, keep offering it regularly. If your baby has severe eczema or another food allergy, talk to your pediatrician first. Call 911 right away for swelling of the lips or face, trouble breathing, or repeated vomiting.

name: Shrimp
intro: A shellfish the FDA lists as a “Best Choice” for children because it’s low in mercury.

serving.text: Puree or mince cooked shrimp very finely and mix into a puree.
Chop cooked shrimp into very small pieces.
Cut into small pieces.

choking: Whole shrimp are firm and round; chop finely. Cook until opaque.
allergenNote: Shellfish is a common food allergen. Introduce it early, around 6 months, once your baby has had a few other first foods. Start with a small amount, offer only one new allergen at a time, and watch for a reaction. Once your baby tolerates it, keep offering it regularly. If your baby has severe eczema or another food allergy, talk to your pediatrician first. Call 911 right away for swelling of the lips or face, trouble breathing, or repeated vomiting.

name: Lentils
intro: An affordable plant protein. The CDC lists beans and lentils as plant sources of iron.

serving.text: Cook red lentils until very soft and mash or puree.
Offer thick, mashed lentils your baby can scoop.
Serve soft lentils in family meals.

choking: Low risk when cooked very soft and mashed.

name: Black beans
intro: Beans are a plant source of iron and protein (CDC).

serving.text: Cook until very soft and mash or puree, with no whole beans left.
Mash or flatten each bean.
Flatten or mash beans until your child chews well.

choking: Whole beans are a choking hazard (CDC). Always mash or flatten them.

name: Tofu
intro: A soft, mild plant protein. The CDC lists tofu as a plant source of iron.

serving.text: Mash soft tofu, or offer finger-sized strips of firm tofu that are soft enough to squash easily between your thumb and finger.
Offer small cubes.
Serve small cubes or crumbles.

choking: Low risk when soft.
allergenNote: Soy is a common food allergen. Introduce it early, around 6 months, once your baby has had a few other first foods. Start with a small amount, offer only one new allergen at a time, and watch for a reaction. Once your baby tolerates it, keep offering it regularly. If your baby has severe eczema or another food allergy, talk to your pediatrician first. Call 911 right away for swelling of the lips or face, trouble breathing, or repeated vomiting.

name: Peanut butter
intro: Introducing peanut early can help lower the chance of a peanut allergy (AAP).

serving.text: Thin smooth peanut butter with warm water, breast milk or formula, or stir a little into oatmeal or a fruit puree.
Spread very thinly on toast strips, or keep stirring into foods.
Spread thinly on toast or crackers.

choking: Never give spoonfuls or chunks of peanut butter, or whole or chopped peanuts (CDC). Always thin it or spread it thinly.
allergenNote: Peanut is one of the most common food allergens. Introduce it early, around 6 months, once your baby has had a few other first foods. Start with a small amount, offer only one new allergen at a time, and watch for a reaction. Once your baby tolerates it, keep offering it regularly. If your baby has severe eczema or another food allergy, talk to your pediatrician first. If your baby has severe eczema or an egg allergy, your pediatrician may suggest testing first. Call 911 right away for swelling of the lips or face, trouble breathing, or repeated vomiting.

name: Almond butter
intro: A smooth nut butter that’s an easy way to introduce tree nuts.

serving.text: Thin with warm water, breast milk or formula, or stir into oatmeal or a puree.
Spread very thinly on toast strips.
Spread thinly on toast or crackers.

choking: Never give spoonfuls or chunks of nut butter, or whole or chopped nuts (CDC).
allergenNote: Tree nuts are a common food allergen. Introduce it early, around 6 months, once your baby has had a few other first foods. Start with a small amount, offer only one new allergen at a time, and watch for a reaction. Once your baby tolerates it, keep offering it regularly. If your baby has severe eczema or another food allergy, talk to your pediatrician first. Call 911 right away for swelling of the lips or face, trouble breathing, or repeated vomiting.

name: Tahini
intro: Smooth sesame seed paste, an easy way to introduce sesame.

serving.text: Stir a little into a puree, yogurt or oatmeal.
Swirl into foods or spread very thinly on toast strips.
Spread thinly, or use in hummus.

choking: Thin tahini or spread it thinly. Avoid whole seeds and spoonfuls of seed butter (CDC).
allergenNote: Sesame is a common food allergen. Introduce it early, around 6 months, once your baby has had a few other first foods. Start with a small amount, offer only one new allergen at a time, and watch for a reaction. Once your baby tolerates it, keep offering it regularly. If your baby has severe eczema or another food allergy, talk to your pediatrician first. Call 911 right away for swelling of the lips or face, trouble breathing, or repeated vomiting.

name: Red lentils
intro: Quick-cooking split lentils that turn soft and creamy. The CDC lists beans and lentils as plant sources of iron.

serving.text: Simmer until very soft, then mash or puree.
Offer thick, mashed red lentils your baby can scoop, or mix into vegetable mashes.
Serve soft red lentils in family meals like dal or soup.

choking: Low risk when cooked very soft and mashed.

name: Iron-fortified infant cereal
intro: Iron-fortified infant cereal is an easy way to add iron (CDC).

serving.text: Mix with breast milk, formula or water into a smooth, thin cereal, and thicken it as your baby gets used to it.
Make it thicker, or mix into fruit purees.
Keep using it in oatmeal, pancakes or muffins.

choking: Low risk. Never put cereal in a bottle.

name: Oats
intro: A warm, filling whole grain.

serving.text: Grind rolled oats into a fine powder and cook into smooth oatmeal.
Serve thicker oatmeal, or soft baked oatmeal fingers.
Serve oatmeal or baked oat bars.

choking: Low risk when cooked soft. Avoid granola bars and dry oat snacks (CDC).

name: Rice
intro: A soft grain that works in many family meals.

serving.text: Cook very soft and blend with a puree.
Serve soft, sticky rice your baby can pick up, or press into small balls.
Serve soft rice from family meals.

choking: Low risk when cooked soft.

name: Pasta
intro: Soft-cooked pasta is easy to hold and fun to eat.

serving.text: Cook large shapes until very soft, like fusilli or penne, so your baby can hold them.
Offer small, soft shapes.
Serve soft pasta from family meals.

choking: Low risk when cooked soft.
allergenNote: Wheat is a common food allergen. Introduce it early, around 6 months, once your baby has had a few other first foods. Start with a small amount, offer only one new allergen at a time, and watch for a reaction. Once your baby tolerates it, keep offering it regularly. If your baby has severe eczema or another food allergy, talk to your pediatrician first. Call 911 right away for swelling of the lips or face, trouble breathing, or repeated vomiting.

name: Bread
intro: Lightly toasted bread strips are an easy first finger food.

serving.text: Offer lightly toasted bread strips with a thin spread, like mashed avocado.
Offer small pieces of lightly toasted bread.
Serve small pieces or sandwich squares.

choking: Soft, doughy bread can form a sticky ball. Lightly toast it. Avoid breads with seeds, nut pieces or whole grain kernels (CDC).
allergenNote: Wheat is a common food allergen. Introduce it early, around 6 months, once your baby has had a few other first foods. Start with a small amount, offer only one new allergen at a time, and watch for a reaction. Once your baby tolerates it, keep offering it regularly. If your baby has severe eczema or another food allergy, talk to your pediatrician first. Call 911 right away for swelling of the lips or face, trouble breathing, or repeated vomiting.

name: Brown rice
intro: A whole-grain rice with a nutty taste and a little more texture than white rice.

serving.text: Cook very soft and blend with a puree.
Serve soft, well-cooked brown rice your baby can pick up, or press it into small balls.
Serve soft brown rice from family meals.

choking: Low risk when cooked very soft.

name: Quinoa
intro: A small, quick-cooking seed that’s eaten like a grain.

serving.text: Rinse well, cook until very soft, then blend or stir into purees.
Serve soft quinoa mixed into mashes, or pressed into small patties.
Serve soft quinoa in family meals, like bowls and salads.

choking: Low risk when cooked soft.

name: Yogurt
intro: Plain whole-milk yogurt can be offered from about 6 months (CDC).

serving.text: Serve plain whole-milk yogurt on a spoon, or swirl in fruit puree.
Serve plain yogurt with mashed fruit.
Serve plain yogurt; cow’s milk as a drink can start now too.

choking: Low risk.
allergenNote: Milk is one of the most common food allergens. Introduce it early, around 6 months, once your baby has had a few other first foods. Start with a small amount, offer only one new allergen at a time, and watch for a reaction. Once your baby tolerates it, keep offering it regularly. If your baby has severe eczema or another food allergy, talk to your pediatrician first. Call 911 right away for swelling of the lips or face, trouble breathing, or repeated vomiting.

name: Cheese
intro: Pasteurized cheese can be offered from about 6 months.

serving.text: Offer finely shredded cheese, or thin, flat slices.
Offer shredded cheese or small, thin pieces.
Serve shredded cheese or small pieces.

choking: Large chunks of cheese, especially string cheese, are a choking hazard (CDC). Shred or cut it thin.
allergenNote: Milk is one of the most common food allergens. Introduce it early, around 6 months, once your baby has had a few other first foods. Start with a small amount, offer only one new allergen at a time, and watch for a reaction. Once your baby tolerates it, keep offering it regularly. If your baby has severe eczema or another food allergy, talk to your pediatrician first. Call 911 right away for swelling of the lips or face, trouble breathing, or repeated vomiting.
